prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Federal Employment Viewpoint Survey (FEVS)
Description: The Office of Personnel Management Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (OPM FEVS) is an organizational climate survey and assesses how employees jointly experience the policies, practices, and procedures characteristic of their agency and its leadership. Results from the OPM FEVS offers insights into whether, and to what extent, workplace conditions characterizing successful organizations are present in Federal agencies, information important to successful organizational change and development initiatives.
URL: https://opm.gov/fevs

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research this dataset comprehensively. Let me start with several searches covering different angles.I have solid foundational material. Let me research a few more angles: recent status/cancellation of the survey, typical users like Best Places to Work, and preservation efforts.# Research Report: OPM Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS)

## 1. Verification of Your Information — With One Correction

Your description and URL are accurate, but the **title is slightly wrong**: the official name is the **Federal *Employee* Viewpoint Survey**, not "Federal Employment Viewpoint Survey." The description you quoted matches OPM's own language verbatim, and **https://opm.gov/fevs** is the correct official landing page. The dataset is cataloged on data.gov as identifier **OPM-ES-0019** ("Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS) Public Data File"), published by the U.S. Office of Personnel Management under a U.S. public domain license.

---

## 2. Who Publishes It

- **Publisher:** The **U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM)**, specifically its survey program office (contact: evs@opm.gov; data contact: datadrivenworkforce@opm.gov).
- **Contractor:** **Westat**, a research firm based in Rockville, MD, has been the primary technical contractor since 2004. Westat hosts the **FEVS Online Analysis and Reporting Tool (WesDaX/Data Xplorer)**, a password-protected system through which agencies access their reports and run "Analysis on Demand" (cross-tabs, trends, frequencies).
- **Relationship to agencies:** OPM centrally administers the survey *on behalf of* executive agencies; participating in FEVS satisfies each agency's separate statutory obligation to survey its own employees (the "Annual Employee Survey," or AES).

---

## 3. Legal Authority and Mandate

This is a **statutorily mandated** dataset, which matters greatly for preservation:

- **Statute:** **Section 1128 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2004 (Pub. L. 108-136, enacted Nov. 24, 2003)**, codified at **5 U.S.C. 7101 note**. It requires each executive agency (as defined in 5 U.S.C. 105) to survey employees *annually* on leadership/management practices and employee satisfaction, directs OPM to prescribe common questions for cross-agency comparability, and requires results be **made public and posted on agency websites** (with a national-security exception).
- **Implementing regulation:** **5 CFR part 250, subpart C ("Employee Surveys")**, issued as a final rule Aug. 24, 2006, effective Jan. 1, 2007, and revised in 2016. It prescribes the core Annual Employee Survey items (16 questions in the current version, embedded within the longer FEVS instrument) and the 120-day public posting requirement.
- **Earlier authority:** The pre-2007 surveys ran under OPM's general research authorities (5 U.S.C. 1103, 4702; Executive Order 13197). The 2017 Privacy Act System of Records Notice (SORN) for the survey cites 5 U.S.C. 1103, 4702, and 7101 note.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act:** The survey operates under OMB control numbers (e.g., 3206-0253 historically; a 2026 Federal Register notice appears under "3206-NEW").

---

## 4. History and Evolution

| Period | Development |
|---|---|
| 1979 | Ancestor: **Federal Employee Attitudes Survey**, first administered the year OPM was created under the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978. |
| 2002 | **Federal Human Capital Survey (FHCS)** first administered governmentwide. |
| 2004–2008 | FHCS administered **biennially** (2004, 2006, 2008). |
| 2010 | Renamed **Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS)**, refocused on "actionable items," and switched to **annual** administration (typically each May–June). |
| 2016 | New disclosure-avoidance methodology introduced for the Public Release Data File (see §6). |
| 2022 | 13 diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility (DEIA) questions added under the Biden administration. |
| Feb 2025 | OPM memo: DEIA and gender-related questions to be removed; a "poor performers" question reinstated; survey delayed; prior reports (2012–2024) to be flagged as "inconsistent" with new executive orders. |
| Aug 15, 2025 | **OPM cancelled the 2025 FEVS entirely** — the first missed administration since 2002 — citing workforce "realignment" and recalibration to administration objectives. This drew congressional protests (e.g., a Sept. 2025 letter from Sens. Van Hollen and Peters and Rep. Walkinshaw) noting the statutory annual-survey requirement remains in force. |
| Nov–Dec 2025 | The nonprofit **Partnership for Public Service** fielded an independent **Public Service Viewpoint Survey** to fill the data gap. |
| 2026 | OPM proposed via Federal Register rulemaking to **reduce the mandated AES core from 16 to 10 questions and end central administration**, shifting survey administration to individual agencies, with OPM providing only a "common form." |

**Preservation implication:** The time series (2002–2024, with a 2025 gap and a planned instrument redesign) is now a *discontinuity risk*. The 2024 cycle is the last under the "classic" design.

---

## 5. Scope, Methodology, and Data Characteristics

- **Population:** Full-time and part-time, permanent, non-seasonal, non-political employees of executive branch agencies. It is one of the largest organizational climate surveys in the world — the **2024 administration drew over 647,000 respondents**; historically it has covered ~80+ agencies with response rates generally in the 30–50% range. (Some large components — e.g., parts of the Intelligence Community, USPS — run their own surveys.)
- **Instrument:** Likert-type, mark-one, and mark-all-that-apply items covering employee engagement, job/organization satisfaction, leadership, supervision, work environment, work-life, performance culture, and demographics. Indices include the Employee Engagement Index, Global Satisfaction Index, Performance Confidence Index, and (2022–2024) a DEIA index.
- **Weighting:** Three-step process — base weights (inverse of selection probability), nonresponse adjustment within agency subgroups, and **raking** to population distributions by sex, sub-agency, and minority status. Precision estimated via Taylor linearization; replicate weights (JKn jackknife) for Analysis on Demand. Full details in annual **Technical Reports**.
- **Quality control:** Independent dual-programming verification of all report figures by Westat; reports are 508-compliant.

---

## 6. Data Products and Access

1. **Public Release Data Files (PRDF):** De-identified, respondent-level CSV files downloadable by year from opm.gov/fevs/public-data-file, with codebooks (Excel) and Read Me documentation. Public domain license; mirrored on data.gov.
   - **Disclosure avoidance (since 2016):** Small work units are collapsed (e.g., 2023: agency-level only, ≥750 respondents; 2024: one level below agency, ≥500); demographics are coarsened (e.g., age to Over/Under 40); and "at-risk" cells (fewer than 5 respondents with an identical demographic/work-unit combination) have demographic values masked so any attempted re-identification matches at least 5 individuals. Researchers should know the PRDF is *not* the raw file — masking affects subgroup analyses.
2. **Governmentwide Management Reports** (annual PDFs with results by agency, demographics, occupation).
3. **Agency/sub-agency/demographic/occupational-series reports**, distributed to agencies via WesDaX.
4. **Technical Reports** documenting instrument, sample design, weighting, and masking (annual PDFs).
5. **Analysis on Demand** (agency users only, via WesDaX).
6. **Preservation mirrors:** The **DataLumos archive** (ICPSR's community data-preservation project) holds the 2024 PRDF CSV (~139 MB), codebook, Read Me, and indices guide — created specifically because of continuity concerns after the 2025 cancellation.

---

## 7. Typical Users

- **Agency leaders, CHCOs, and HR offices** — the primary intended users — for organizational change, management improvement, and Human Capital Framework accountability.
- **Congress and oversight bodies** (GAO, MSPB, House Oversight and Senate HSGAC) for agency accountability; FEVS results have figured in congressional hearings.
- **The Partnership for Public Service and Boston Consulting Group**, whose annual **Best Places to Work in the Federal Government rankings** (produced since 2003) are built mostly on FEVS data — the engagement score is a weighted formula of three FEVS items (recommend as good place to work; job satisfaction; organization satisfaction).
- **Academic and policy researchers** in public administration, organizational psychology, and labor economics — the PRDF is one of the most-used federal microdata products for studying public-sector motivation, leadership, telework, and turnover intention.
- **Journalists, unions, and advocacy groups** tracking morale during shutdowns, administration transitions, and workforce policy changes.
- **Federal employees and job seekers** using Best Places to Work to compare agencies.

---

## 8. Public Benefits

- **Statutory transparency:** The 2003 law expressly requires public posting of results; FEVS operationalizes public accountability for how ~2 million federal workers are managed.
- **Cross-agency comparability:** Common core items allow benchmarking across the entire executive branch and over two decades — a rare longitudinal panel of organizational climate.
- **Evidence-based management:** Agencies use results to target interventions; OPM links them to the Human Capital Framework.
- **Research infrastructure:** The public-domain microdata with documented methodology supports independent replication and scholarship at zero cost.
- **Civic accountability:** Rankings and press coverage translate the data into public-facing measures of government performance.

---

## 9. Risks and Considerations for Preservationists, Librarians, and Activists

- **Political discontinuity:** The 2025 cancellation, removal of DEIA items, retroactive flagging of 2012–2024 reports as "inconsistent" with executive orders, and the proposed end of centralized administration mean **content on opm.gov may be altered or removed retroactively** — an active reason to archive now.
- **Series break:** Any post-redesign instrument will not be strictly comparable to 2002–2024; preserving codebooks and technical reports is as important as preserving data files.
- **Masking limits:** The PRDF's disclosure avoidance (collapsed work units, coarsened demographics, 5-person cell rule) constrains small-agency and intersectional analyses; researchers needing finer detail historically needed agency-level reports or WesDaX access.
- **Legal vulnerability:** Although 5 U.S.C. 7101 note mandates annual surveys and public posting, the 2025 experience shows enforcement is effectively political; congressional letters (Sept. 2025) document this tension.
- **What to capture:** PRDF CSVs + codebooks + Read Mes (all years), annual Governmentwide Management Reports, Technical Reports, the survey instruments themselves, the 5 CFR 250 subpart C regulation text, the 2017 SORN, and the 2025–2026 Federal Register notices and CHCO memos documenting the changes. DataLumos already holds 2024; the Wayback Machine holds opm.gov/fevs captures.

---

## Key Sources

- OPM FEVS site and About page: opm.gov/fevs, opm.gov/fevs/about
- 2024 FEVS Technical Report (methodology, weighting, masking): opm.gov/fevs/reports/technical-reports
- Statute: Pub. L. 108-136 §1128 (5 U.S.C. 7101 note); regulation: 5 CFR part 250 subpart C (71 FR 49990, Aug. 24, 2006)
- Privacy Act SORN: Federal Register, Dec. 5, 2017
- 2025 cancellation memo: OPM GovDelivery bulletin, Aug. 15, 2025; coverage in Federal News Network, GovExec, Washington Post
- Congressional concern: Van Hollen/Peters/Walkinshaw letter, Sept. 29, 2025
- 2026 restructuring proposal: Federal Register, July 2, 2026 (OMB Control No. 3206-NEW)
- Best Places to Work methodology: bestplacestowork.org
- Preservation copy: DataLumos, "Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS) 2024" (datalumos.org, project 248623)

I'll build on my prior research with additional targeted searches on OPM staffing, the 2026 regulatory changes, and current site status.One more check on the status of the historical public data files themselves.# Risk Assessment: OPM Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS)

This assessment draws on my prior dataset research plus new findings on OPM's 2025–2026 restructuring. The overall picture is one of the most severe disruption profiles possible short of outright deletion: the 2025 survey was cancelled, historical reports were retroactively redacted under executive orders, the agency lost a third of its staff including its entire data-management office, and OPM has formally announced it will never centrally administer FEVS again.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence by level:**

- **Gone / High Risk:** The FEVS homepage (opm.gov/fevs) now carries a banner stating OPM is "in the process of rescinding or revising reports, tools, files and other materials posted on this website" per EOs 14151 and 14168, and that prior DEI/gender materials "should be considered rescinded." The Feb. 28, 2025 memo directed that reports from **2012–2024 be marked "inconsistent"** with the EOs and that DEIA/gender content be removed from the site and the WesDaX analysis tool. Public Release Data Files are still listed by year on opm.gov/fevs/public-data-file, so bulk removal has not (yet) occurred.
- **Moderate Risk:** Confirmed, documented alterations: the **2023 and 2024 Technical Reports** and the **2024 Governmentwide Management Report** were reissued as "REVISED EDITION APRIL 2025" with survey items 72–84 (the 13 DEIA items) and the sex/gender item **redacted in place** — i.e., data elements that existed in prior-cycle publications have been removed from the versions now served at the primary URL. The DataLumos/ICPSR archive holds a pre-redaction copy of the 2024 PRDF specifically because of this.
- **No Known Issue:** Does not apply — alterations are confirmed.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** Data files for prior cycles remain downloadable, but elements of the historical record hosted at the primary location have already been redacted and the site openly states revision is ongoing, meaning further removal is likely. (If OPM pulls the revised-era files or older PRDFs, this escalates to High/Gone — a real possibility given the announced end of the program.)

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence by level:**

- **Gone:** On July 9, 2026, OPM Director Scott Kupor's memo to all agency heads stated: **"OPM will no longer administer the Federal Employee Viewpoint Survey (FEVS)"** — agencies must run their own surveys and submit results to OPM/OMB within 90 days; each agency "may determine the manner and content of its public disclosure." FedWeek and GovExec report the guidance **does not commit OPM to issuing a governmentwide report or public data file** of the kind produced for two decades. The 2025 cycle — the last under the classic design — was cancelled outright (Aug. 15, 2025), the first missed administration since 2002.
- **High Risk:** Alternatively: a statutory annual deadline was missed (2025), collection was skipped, and the legacy ICR (3206-0253) was replaced by a new "3206-NEW" common-form collection with no centralized publication commitment.
- **Moderate / No Known Issue:** Do not apply.

**Selected level: Gone** — for the dataset as it has existed (a centrally administered, governmentwide, OPM-published survey and public data file). Employee surveying will continue in decentralized, agency-controlled form under the statute, but the FEVS data product at opm.gov is terminated, and there is no commitment to a consolidated public dataset for 2026 or beyond. A grader who treats the successor agency-level collections as continuation could justify High Risk instead; either way this is the most endangered category.

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence by level:**

- **High Risk:** Documented reductions in granularity and frequency: the mandated core was cut from **16 questions to 10** (11 removed, 5 added, per the July 2, 2026 proposed rule); the **2025 cycle was skipped entirely**; decentralized administration eliminates the standardized instrument, weighting, and masking methodology that ensured cross-agency comparability; and the historical instrument documentation itself has been redacted (items 72–84 now appear as "[Redacted]" in the 2023/2024 technical reports). The 2002–2024 trend series is permanently broken.
- **Moderate Risk:** Would apply if changes were only proposed — they are not; cancellation and instrument changes are implemented/announced.
- **Gone:** Arguable, since the governmentwide product is terminated.

**Selected level: High Risk.** Granularity, comparability, and frequency have all been measurably reduced; the residual agency-level collections mean data quality is degraded rather than wholly extinguished.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence by level:**

- **No Known Issue:** FEVS rests on one of the clearer statutory mandates in federal data: **Section 1128 of the FY2004 NDAA (Pub. L. 108-136; 5 U.S.C. 7101 note)** explicitly requires *annual* employee surveys of executive agencies, directs OPM to prescribe common questions, and requires results be **publicly posted**; implementing regulations exist at **5 CFR part 250, subpart C**. There is no true substitute collection (the Partnership for Public Service's independent 2025 survey is a partial stopgap).
- **Moderate/High Risk:** Would apply only if the mandate were vague or substitutable — it is not. The 2026 proposed rule reduces required questions and ends central administration, but the underlying statute is unchanged and cannot be repealed by regulation.

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** The statutory authorization is explicit, names what must be collected, and has no alternatives. (Caveat: the 2025 cancellation despite this mandate — protested in the Sept. 29, 2025 Van Hollen/Peters/Walkinshaw letter — shows the statute provides weak practical protection, but the rubric measures the legal foundation itself, which is strong.)

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence by level:**

- **High Risk:** OPM shrank from **~3,110 to ~2,000 employees — 1,069 departures (about one-third)**, exceeding both the "1,000 or more staff lost" and (nearly) the 40% thresholds; federal contracting staff were cut roughly in half (1,200 → ~600). RIFs **entirely eliminated OPM's Human Capital Data Management and Modernization office** — the component managing OPM's large data assets — plus the Center for Leadership Development, procurement, and communications/web teams. Leadership changed: acting director Charles Ezell, then Scott Kupor confirmed July 14, 2025. Internal direction in January 2025 ordered planning for a **70% cut** and a stop to all non-statutory work.
- **Moderate Risk:** Numerically the ~34% loss also fits 10–39%, but the ≥1,000 headcount criterion and wholesale elimination of the data office squarely trigger High.
- **Gone:** Not applicable — the agency survives.

**Selected level: High Risk.**

## 6. Policy

**Evidence by level:**

- **High Risk:** This category reads as if written about FEVS: a **Presidential Action-driven** information collection (changes explicitly tied to **EO 14151 and EO 14168**); a **negative policy note on the site** (the rescission banner on opm.gov/fevs and "inconsistent with EOs" flags on 2012–2024 reports); and **significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities** (DEIA question removal, "poor performers" question reinstated, 2025 delay-then-cancellation, decentralization, 16→10 questions).
- **Gone:** Centralized collection/publication terminated — also arguably applicable (see Future Data Availability).
- **Moderate / No Known Issue:** Do not apply; changes are implemented, not merely proposed.

**Selected level: High Risk** (consistent with treating the termination itself under Future Data Availability; a grader could reasonably score this Gone for the same reason).

---

## Summary

- **Historical Data Availability: Moderate Risk** — files still up, but prior-cycle reports redacted in place and site-wide revision ongoing
- **Future Data Availability: Gone** — 2025 cancelled; OPM has permanently ended central administration with no governmentwide public data product committed
- **Data Quality: High Risk** — skipped cycle, core instrument cut 16→10, loss of cross-agency comparability and trend continuity
- **Statutory Context: No Known Issue** — explicit, detailed statutory mandate (Pub. L. 108-136 §1128) with no substitutes; statute remains intact
- **Staffing and Funding: High Risk** — ~1,069 OPM staff lost (~one-third), data-management office eliminated, leadership replaced
- **Policy: High Risk** — EO-driven ICR changes, rescission notices on site, and program restructuring aligned to administration priorities

**Bottom line for preservationists:** FEVS is a worst-case-but-still-salvageable dataset. The 2002–2024 series is the final complete record of the centralized program; opm.gov has already demonstrated willingness to alter historical documents in place. Immediate capture of all PRDFs, codebooks, technical reports, and management reports — plus verification against the pre-redaction DataLumos mirror — is strongly warranted.
